description: Xelas is the great Transformer of Coast Salish tradition, a benevolent culture hero who traveled the Pacific Northwest reshaping the world. He turned the changeling beings of the myth age into their present forms and set the natural order, remembered as Xáays among the Squamish and Xa:ls in Halkomelem.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; native-languages.org; Lummi/Squamish/Halkomelem sources
research_notes: Attested. Xelas is a genuine Coast Salish Transformer figure known by different names across Coast Salish languages: Xáays (Squamish), Xa:ls (Halkomelem), Xelas (Lummi). He traveled with helpers turning the flawed beings of the myth age into present animals, plants, and landforms; his work explains the current shape of the world.

description: Bukwus (Bakwas) is the wild man of the woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a small, green-skinned ghost-king with a skeletal face and long curving nose. He prowls the forests, whistling to lure the living toward the realm of the dead; some accounts name him the husband of Dzunukwa, the Cannibal Woman.
source: Boas Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) ethnography; Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology
research_notes: Attested. Bakwas/Bukwus is documented in Boas's Kwakiutl ethnography as king of the ghosts, a small green forest spirit with a skeletal face and long nose. He lures the living toward the land of the dead; some versions make him Dzunukwa's husband. His masked figure appears in the winter ceremonial.

description: Although often filed under Coast Salish, the Ho-ho-e-ap-bess are the Makah Twin Transformers, the Two Men Who Changed Things, who in Makah legend traveled the world reshaping beings and landscape into their present forms. Brothers of the sun and the moon, their journeys explain the world as it is today.
source: native-languages.org Makah Legends (Hohoeapbess)
research_notes: Tribe misattribution found. The Ho-ho-e-ap-bess (Hohoeapbess) are Makah, not Coast Salish: Twin Transformer brothers called the 'Two Men Who Changed Things,' brothers of the sun and moon, who reshaped the world. Native-languages.org lists them under Makah legends. Correct tribe noted in description.

description: In Wasco (Chinookan) tradition, the Five Wolf Brothers appear as traveling companions in a tale cycle in which Coyote places the stars and orders the sky. Variants tell of rival sets of brothers whose contest produced the winds; the wolf brothers embody the strength of the pack, which Chinookan peoples respected in their storytelling.
source: Wasco/Chinookan oral tradition; mythfolklore UN-Textbook Chinook tales
research_notes: Attested. The Five Wolf Brothers appear in Wasco (Chinookan) tradition; variants connect them to Coyote's placing of the stars and to the Chinook Wind-brothers tale. Wasco is a Chinookan-speaking tribe of The Dalles, Oregon. The pack motif reflects the wolf's cultural prominence as hunter and ally.

description: Wolf is one of the four matrilineal clans of the Coast Tsimshian, called Laxgyibuu, and a principal crest whose legend holds that the wolf is the land equivalent of the killer whale. Wolf-clan spirit beings, ancestors who came from the supernatural world, are honored in crest carvings, songs, and potlatch regalia and guard the clan's territory and identity.
source: AMNH Northwest Coast exhibit; Wikipedia Tsimshian mythology; Tsimshian clan studies
research_notes: Attested. Wolf (Laxgyibuu) is one of the four matrilineal Coast Tsimshian clans. Crest lore holds that the wolf is the land equivalent of the killer whale, reflecting parallel social structures. Wolf-clan spirit beings and crests are documented at AMNH and in Tsimshian clan studies; a Gitsontk-specific origin tale is not separately confirmed.

description: The name Chulyen belongs to the Dena'ina, an Athabaskan people of south-central Alaska, where Chulyen is the raven trickster and transformer of the Kenai Peninsula, not a Nuu-chah-nulth figure. Nuu-chah-nulth tradition gives the raven's role to its own culture hero, while the Dena'ina raven cycle tells how Chulyen stole fire and shaped the land.
source: Dena'ina oral tradition (Kenai Peninsula); Alaska Native story collections (Kalifornsky)
research_notes: Tribe misattribution found. Chulyen is a Dena'ina (Alaskan Athabaskan) raven trickster of the Kenai Peninsula, not a Nuu-chah-nulth figure. Nuu-chah-nulth raven stories belong to their own culture hero. The Dena'ina raven cycle is documented in Alaska Native story collections (e.g., Kalifornsky).

description: Not independently attested as a named spirit in Coast Salish folklore. Cranes are minor figures in Northwestern narrative: in Salishan Plateau traditions Crane is a wise helper and companion of Coyote, and in other Northwest tales he stretches his long neck to form a bridge for fleeing children. No distinct crane being is recorded for the Coast Salish peoples.
source: Adamson, Folk-Tales of the Coast Salish (1934); Salishan Plateau Crane narratives
research_notes: Unattested. No named crane being is recorded specifically for the Coast Salish. The main collection, Adamson's Folk-Tales of the Coast Salish (1934), does not feature a crane figure. Crane appears as Coyote's companion in Salishan Plateau tales (Coeur d'Alene 'Landscape Traveled by Coyote and Crane') and as a neck-bridge helper in some Northwestern stories.

description: Tlingit storytellers recount how Raven made the tides, teaching the ocean to rise and fall. In the tale of how the tides began, the tide-water is kept by an old woman, in some versions Raven's grandmother, and Raven tricks her into releasing the water so the beaches can be walked and the sea fished.
source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909); sacred-texts.org
research_notes: Attested as tale. The Tlingit story of how the tides began explains the origin of the tides: Raven steals or persuades an old woman, in some versions his grandmother, to release the tide-water. 'Tide Woman' as a named deity is not standard; the keeper-woman role is the closest match. Source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909).

description: Bear Woman is the heart of the Bear Mother story told by the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian. A girl who mocked bears was taken by a bear and married the bear chief, discovering that bears live like people in a great house; her children became the ancestors of bear clans, and the tale explains why bears and humans are kin and why the bear is honored.
source: Bear Mother tale; orderwhitemoon.org; Haida/Tlingit/Tsimshian oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. The Bear Mother story is shared by Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian: a berry-picking girl marries the bear chief and bears him children, and bears are revealed as kin. The tale is depicted on totem poles and in a Charles Edenshaw carving (c. 1900) and explains bear taboos and the bear clan.

description: In Kwakwaka'wakw belief the killer whale rules the undersea world, attended by sea lions as slaves and dolphins as warriors, and may carry the soul of a deceased chief. In the Siwidi story the ancestor travels the sea kingdom with killer-whale attendants in the copper house of Ḵumugwe; the orca is a high-ranking clan crest.
source: Wikipedia 'Orca'; AMNH Kwakwaka'wakw exhibit (Siwidi); Northwest Coast art sources
research_notes: Attested. For the Kwakwaka'wakw the killer whale rules the undersea world (sea lions as slaves, dolphins as warriors) and may embody the soul of a deceased chief. In the Siwidi story the ancestor is taken to Kumugwe's copper house with killer-whale attendants. The orca is a high-ranking crest. Sources: Wikipedia 'Orca'; AMNH exhibit.

description: Hatsenas is the Tsimshian bird of good omen, a robin-like messenger sent from heaven and supernatural father of the hero Asdiwal. In the Asdiwal myth he visits a starving widow and her daughter, brings them food, weds the younger woman, and equips his son with magic gifts; Lévi-Strauss read him as a mediator of the middle heavens.
source: Lévi-Strauss, 'The Story of Asdiwal' (1958); Boas, Tsimshian Mythology (1912)
research_notes: Attested. Hatsenas is described by Boas as a Tsimshian 'bird of good omen' (the name means 'luck'), a robin-like messenger from heaven, and in the Asdiwal myth the supernatural father of Asdiwal. He provides food during famine and gifts his son magic objects. Analyzed by Lévi-Strauss as a mediator of the atmospheric heavens.

description: Among the Northwest Coast peoples who raised the great cedar poles — Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, and Kwakwaka'wakw — the totem is a system of clan crests: animal and spirit ancestors such as Raven, Eagle, Killer Whale, Bear, Wolf, and Beaver carved on towering monuments. Each figure records a lineage's origin story and rights, witnessed and validated at potlatches.
source: NPS Sitka National Historical Park; Britannica 'Totem pole'
research_notes: Attested as tradition. 'Totem' is not a single creature but the crest system of Northwest Coast peoples. NPS (Sitka) classifies poles as crest, history, legend, or memorial/mortuary poles. Crest figures record clan ancestry and are validated at potlatches. Britannica and NPS provide solid documentation.

description: The Beaver is a Tsimshian crest whose origin is told as the Gitsalas legend of the Beaver Crest, recorded by William Beynon. A woman dammed a stream to swim in it and refused to leave, and she was transformed, her leather apron becoming the beaver's tail. Beaver is a clan ancestor of the Eagle division and a figure of diligence and persistence.
source: Beynon 1948 'Origin of the Beaver Crest' (Tsimsyan); Tsimshian oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. The Origin of the Beaver Crest (Gitsalas/Gillodzar, Eagle clan) was recorded by William Beynon from informant John Tait in 1948. A widespread Tsimshian story tells of a woman who dammed a stream to swim and was transformed, her leather apron becoming the beaver's tail. Beaver is also a crest animal among the Tlingit (S'eek).

description: Raven is the great culture hero of the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka), a benevolent transformer and trickster who gave the people fire, light, and the shape of the world. In Nuu-chah-nulth tradition he works alongside the Twin Transformers Kwe'kustepsep, who changed people, animals, and the land into their present forms.
source: native-languages.org Nootka Legends; Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Nuu-chah-nulth Raven culture hero. The spelling 'Guguyni' is not confirmed in the sources located; the Nuu-chah-nulth raven is the benevolent transformer and trickster paired with the Twin Transformers Kwe'kustepsep. Raven brought fire, light, and the shaped world. Source: native-languages.org Nootka legends.

description: Kalga Jaad, 'Ice Woman,' is a primordial ancestress of Haida oral tradition, counted among the ancient beings who existed when the glaciers covered the land. She is remembered as one of the very old figures whose presence links the Haida people to the deep past of the world's making.
source: Haida oral tradition; Swanton-era Haida ethnographic texts
research_notes: Attested (conservative). Kalga Jaad ('Ice Woman') is a primordial Haida ancestress of the deep past, associated with the ice age and glaciers. Framed conservatively as an ancient being of Haida tradition; she appears in early Haida ethnographic texts (Swanton-era). Further specifics are limited, so the description stays general.

description: Io'i is not a Coast Salish figure but the sister of Blue Jay, the trickster of Chinookan tales told at the lower Columbia River. Blue Jay and Io'i travel together in adventure stories in which Io'i repeatedly saves her foolish brother from the consequences of his boasting and meddling.
source: Chinookan Blue Jay tales; native-languages.org Ioi
research_notes: Tribe misattribution found. Io'i is the sister of Blue Jay, the trickster of Chinookan tales of the lower Columbia, not a Coast Salish figure. Blue Jay and Io'i travel together; Io'i often rescues her boastful brother. Documented in native-languages.org and Chinookan story collections.

description: In the Tsimshian tale 'The Bear Who Married a Woman,' a young woman is courted at night by a suitor with rough palms, and each dawn a larger sea animal lies on the beach. When her mother keeps watch, a red bear rises from the water carrying a whale on each side; discovered, he turns to stone, a supernatural being of the sea.
source: Boas, Tsimshian Mythology (1916) p.19; Ashliman folktexts
research_notes: Attested. Boas recorded 'The Bear Who Married a Woman' (Tsimshian Mythology, 1916, p. 19) from the Gispaxlâ'ts: a widow's daughter tests suitors by palm roughness; the night suitor is a red bear of the sea who brings a larger animal each dawn (halibut, seal, then whales) and turns to stone when seen. A supernatural sea-bear husband.

description: Asdiwal is the hero of a celebrated Tsimshian myth studied by Claude Lévi-Strauss. Son of Ho, who made him magic snowshoes, Asdiwal chases a white bear up a ladder into the sky and finds it is the daughter of the Sun; he wins her through impossible trials and marries her, before his boastfulness brings him ruin.
source: Lévi-Strauss, 'The Story of Asdiwal' (1958); Boas, Tsimshian Mythology
research_notes: Attested. Asdiwal is a Tsimshian hero, son of Ho who made him magic snowshoes; he chases a white bear that is the daughter of the Sun, wins her through trials, and marries her. The myth was analyzed by Claude Lévi-Strauss in 'The Story of Asdiwal' (1958). Four versions were collected by Boas between 1895 and 1916.

description: Brer Possum is a character of African American folktale, one of the animal figures of the Uncle Remus cycle written down by Joel Chandler Harris from stories brought from West Africa by enslaved people. As Brer Rabbit's neighbor he is sly and slow, frequently outwitted yet resilient, a trickster of the American South rather than a Native American figure.
source: Joel Chandler Harris, Uncle Remus (1881); Britannica 'Brer Rabbit'; African American folktale
research_notes: Attested but not Native American. Brer Possum belongs to African American folktale from the Uncle Remus cycle (Joel Chandler Harris, 1880s), rooted in West African trickster stories carried by enslaved people. The possum is one of the animal neighbors of Brer Rabbit. No Native North American possum deity of this kind exists.

description: Wakinyan is the Thunderer of the Lakota, a powerful sky spirit that dwells in the west and appears as a giant bird whose wingbeats roll thunder and whose eye blinks lightning. Wakinyan brings the life-giving rains and, as the enemy of the evil water monsters, keeps the world in balance.
source: native-languages.org Thunderer; Lakota oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Wakinyan is the Lakota/Dakota Thunderer or Thunderbird, a giant bird of the west whose wingbeats make thunder and whose eyes flash lightning. It brings rain and is the enemy of evil water monsters. Documented at native-languages.org and in Lakota oral tradition.

description: In Tsimshian texts from the Nass River, the great Grizzly Bear is the wife of a man — a supernatural bride who fills her husband's house with salmon and uses her stomach as a berry basket. In the companion tale 'The Bear Who Married a Woman,' a human woman becomes the bear chief's wife; bear marriage runs both ways in Tsimshian tradition.
source: Boas, Tsimshian Texts (Nass River dialect); native-languages.org
research_notes: Attested. In Boas's Tsimshian Texts (Nass River dialect), a man marries the great Grizzly Bear, a supernatural wife who fills the house with salmon and eats berries into her own stomach. The paired tale 'The Bear Who Married a Woman' has a woman become the bear chief's wife, so bear marriage runs in both directions in Tsimshian tradition.

description: Salmon Boy is a guardian-spirit tale told by the Nuxalk and many Northwest Coast peoples. A boy who mocked the salmon is taken by the salmon people into their underwater villages, where he lives among them, learns their laws and the songs of the salmon, and returns to teach his people how to honor the fish so that the runs will return.
source: Salmon Boy legend; native-languages.org; Nuxalk oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Salmon Boy is a guardian-spirit tale told by the Nuxalk and widely across the Northwest Coast (also Haida/Tsimshian variants). A boy who disrespected the salmon is taken to the salmon people's village, learns their laws, and returns to teach stewardship. The story underlies salmon ceremonies and resource practices.

description: The Kowi Anukasha are the little people of the Choctaw, spirit dwellers of the forests whose name means 'forest dwellers.' Kindly but quick-tempered, they live in the deep woods and under the ground, and they may help hunters and children; the prankster variant, Bohpoli the 'thrower in the dark,' delights in startling travelers.
source: Choctaw oral tradition; native-languages.org Kowi Anukasha
research_notes: Attested. The Kowi Anukasha (Kowi anúkvsha) are the Choctaw little people, the 'forest dwellers,' related to the trickster Bohpoli ('thrower in the dark'). They live in the woods and under the ground, sometimes helping hunters; they are documented in Choctaw oral tradition and native-languages.org.

description: Alhkw'ntam is the creator of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola), who made the world and set the sun and moon in their boxes in the sky house Nusmata. With the Four Carpenters, his helpers Masmasalanicw, he shaped the land, gave the people their arts, and established the order of the seasons and ceremonial life.
source: Nuxalk (Bella Coola) oral tradition; nuxalk.net; Boas Bella Coola texts
research_notes: Attested. Alhkw'ntam is the Nuxalk (Bella Coola) creator who placed the sun and moon in boxes in the sky house Nusmata and, with the Four Carpenters (Masmasalanicw), shaped the world and gave the people their arts. Documented in Boas's Bella Coola texts and Nuxalk tradition.

description: Yulm is the eldest of the Four Carpenters, the culture-hero craftsmen who assisted the Nuxalk creator Alhkw'ntam in shaping the world. His name lives on in the making of the first bird: Yulm molded a qwaxw from charcoal and set it to fly, giving the Nuxalk the origin of birds and of carving.
source: Nuxalk (Bella Coola) oral tradition; nuxalk.net
research_notes: Attested. Yulm is the eldest of the Four Carpenters who assisted the Nuxalk creator. He is credited with making the first bird (qwaxw) from charcoal. The Four Carpenters are documented in Nuxalk (Bella Coola) origin accounts.

description: In Tsimshian myth the Sun is a celestial chief whose son, Walks-All-Over-The-Sky, carries a burning cedar-bark mask across the heavens each day; sparks from his mouth become the stars and his charcoal-faced brother becomes the moon. In the Asdiwal story the Sun tests suitors for his daughter, who appears on earth as a white bear.
source: Stanford Solar Center 'Walks All Over the Sky'; Boas, Tsimshian Mythology
research_notes: Attested. In Tsimshian myth the Sun is a celestial chief; 'Walks All Over the Sky' tells how his son carries a burning mask across the sky as the sun, his brother becomes the moon, and sparks become stars. In Asdiwal the Sun tests suitors for his daughter, the white bear. Strong documentation (Stanford Solar Center; Boas).

description: Wasgo, the sea wolf, is a powerful being of Haida tradition that moves between ocean and land, part wolf and part killer whale. Capable of seizing a whale and of storming the shore, it appears in crest carvings and pole legends as a creature of great supernatural strength linking the sea and the forest.
source: Haida oral tradition; Wasgo legend pole (Sitka NHP); Haida crest tradition
research_notes: Attested. Wasgo, the sea wolf, is a Haida supernatural being of both ocean and land, sometimes shown seizing whales. It appears as a crest and is remembered in pole legends (a Wasgo legend pole was re-carved at Sitka NHP in 2021). It emphasizes the boundary between sea and forest powers.

description: Mink is the trickster of the Coast Salish, told of among the Saanich, Comox, and Lummi. Compared with Raven he is a negative hero, greedy, reckless, and vain, and his adventures — being swallowed by a whale, running across the sky as the Sun's son, tussling with Devilfish — are cautionary tales of how not to behave.
source: native-languages.org Mink (Saanich/Comox/Lummi); Coast Salish oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as Mink. The specific name 'Qals' is not confirmed in the sources located; the figure is the Coast Salish trickster Mink, told of by the Saanich, Comox, and Lummi. Mink is a negative trickster (greed, vanity, recklessness) whose tales (Mink and Whale, Mink and Devilfish) are cautionary. Source: native-languages.org Mink.

description: Not independently attested as a separate crow being in Tlingit folklore. The raven-crow narrative role of Tlingit myth belongs to Yéil, the Raven culture hero and world-maker whose cycle of adventures includes stealing the light and shaping the world; no distinct female crow trickster is recorded for the Tlingit.
source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts; Sealaska Heritage Institute Raven stories
research_notes: Unattested as crow. No distinct 'crow' being is recorded for the Tlingit; the raven-crow narrative role belongs to Yéil, the Raven culture hero and world-maker (Swanton; Sealaska Heritage Institute). The input likely conflates crow and raven. Marked unattested with Yéil as the closest real analogue.

description: Xelas (Xe Las) is the Transformer of Coast Salish oral tradition who walked the world setting it right in the myth age. He and his helpers changed the flawed beings of that time into the animals and landmarks of today, and Coast Salish peoples trace the present shape of mountains, rivers, and creatures to his journeys.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; native-languages.org; Squamish/Halkomelem sources
research_notes: Attested. Same figure as Xe Las the Changer (slugs 1 and 30 are duplicates in the input). Xelas is the Coast Salish Transformer; the two entries should be merged or deduplicated in the database. Content matches the Squamish Xáays / Halkomelem Xa:ls tradition.

description: Dzunukwa (Dzunuk'wa) is the Cannibal Woman of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a giant wild woman of the deep woods with black tangled hair, a puckered mouth, and a huge cedar-bark basket on her back. She carries off children to eat them but is clumsy and easily outwitted, and her masked figure is a dramatic presence of the winter ceremonial.
source: Brooklyn Museum Dzunuk'wa mask; U'mista Cultural Centre; Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology
research_notes: Attested. Dzunukwa (Dzunuk'wa) is the Cannibal Woman of the Kwakwaka'wakw, a giant wild woman of the woods with a puckered mouth and a cedar-bark basket for carrying children. Clumsy and easily outwitted, she is nonetheless wealth-bearing. Her masks are prominent at the U'mista Cultural Centre and in potlatch collections (e.g., Brooklyn Museum).

description: In Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) legend, the octopus appears in the tale 'Raven Annoys Octopus,' where Raven pesters the octopus people and learns a lesson in respect. An octopus woman with eight long braids digs on the shore with a stick, and the story teaches listeners about meddling and the boundaries of other beings.
source: native-languages.org Nootka Folklore (Raven Annoys Octopus)
research_notes: Attested. The Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) legend 'Raven Annoys Octopus' features Raven pestering the octopus people; an octopus woman has eight braids and digs on the shore. The tale teaches a lesson about meddling. Source: native-languages.org Nootka folklore.

description: Brer Coon is a character of African American folktale from the Uncle Remus cycle compiled by Joel Chandler Harris, a raccoon figure drawn from West African trickster stories carried into the American South. He appears alongside Brer Rabbit and Brer Possum in comic tales of cunning, deceit, and hard lessons.
source: Joel Chandler Harris, Uncle Remus; African American folktale
research_notes: Attested but not Native American. Brer Coon is an African American folktale figure of the Uncle Remus cycle (Joel Chandler Harris), a raccoon trickster drawn from West African traditions. Like Brer Possum, he is not a Native American being; the input's framing should be corrected.

description: Sisiutl is the double-headed sea serpent of the Kwakwaka'wakw, a fearsome supernatural creature whose glance can kill or turn an adversary to stone. It can become an invincible war canoe or a magic belt granting strength, its blood gives warriors invincibility, and it is one of the highest-ranking inherited crests of the winter ceremonial.
source: Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology; Boas Kwakiutl ethnography; Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Sisiutl is the double-headed (sometimes three-headed) sea serpent of the Kwakwaka'wakw; seeing it can cause death or petrify. It can transform into an invincible war canoe or a protective belt, and warriors sought its blood for invincibility. One of the highest inherited crests; documented by Boas and in later overviews.

description: Kóoshdaa káa, the land otter man, is the shapeshifting otter spirit of the Tlingit, a being of the sea edge that appears as a man to lure the drowning and the lost, then transforms them into land otters of its own kind. Related beings appear as 'Watsa among the Tsimshian, and Tlingit hunters treated drowned folk with caution.
source: Wikipedia Kushtaka; godsandmonsters.info; Tlingit oral tradition (Swanton)
research_notes: Attested. Kóoshdaa káa ('land otter man') is a Tlingit shapeshifter that lures the drowning or lost and turns them into land otters. Documented in Tlingit oral tradition (Swanton); parallels include Tsimshian 'Watsa and Dena'ina Nat'ina. Wikipedia and godsandmonsters.info summarize the tradition.
